opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think I got the direction right and the timing wrong, and the reasons for the timing are kind of interesting.

If you go back to around 2017 or 2018, a lot of us working on things like debate and amplification assumed you'd want models to reason at length, critique each other, and get trained on whether that reasoning held up. The intuition was that thinking for longer should help, and RL is how you teach a system to use that extra thinking well. What I underestimated was how much had to be in place before RL on long traces would work at all.

The first piece is the base model. RL is mostly an amplifier: it takes behaviours the model can already produce occasionally and makes them reliable. If the pretrained model almost never produces a correct multi-step chain of reasoning, there's nothing to reinforce. You're searching a huge space with an extremely sparse reward. It took models getting good enough that a decent chain of thought was in the distribution of things they'd sometimes say before the signal was dense enough to learn from. I think I mentally treated that threshold as nearer than it was.

The second piece is reward. Long traces are only useful to train on if you can tell whether the end result is good. Early on, people leaned heavily on learned reward models from human preferences, and those get exploited quickly once you optimise hard against them, especially over long horizons where the model has many chances to find a weird trick. What made things take off was domains with verifiable answers: maths, code with tests, things like that. In hindsight that's obvious, but there was a period where the field was more focused on preference-based fine-tuning and the verifiable-reward recipe wasn't the default.

Third, there's a lot of unglamorous engineering. Long-trace RL is expensive. Sampling lots of long rollouts, keeping training stable, avoiding collapse into degenerate outputs or length gaming, getting the infrastructure efficient enough to be worth it. Those things take years of grinding, and from the outside it can look like nothing is happening right up until it suddenly works.

And there's a sociological piece. Scaling pretraining kept paying off so reliably that the best marginal bet for most labs was just to make the base model bigger. When one lever is working that well, you don't pour resources into a riskier one. Once pretraining returns started looking more expensive to buy, the incentive to push on inference-time compute and RL went up a lot.

So my summary would be: the idea wasn't the bottleneck. The bottlenecks were base-model capability, a reward signal you can't easily game, and the engineering and incentives to make it worth doing. From a safety perspective that matters, because the same issues, especially reward hacking over long horizons, don't go away once things start working. They become more important.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger pretrained models eventually make correct multi-step reasoning common enough to reinforce. It does not connect that threshold to an error-correction ability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those cases where I was wrong about timing, and it's worth being honest about why. When I was at OpenAI, and then at DeepMind, the basic idea was already on the table. You have a language model, it produces a chain of thought, you reward it based on whether it got the right answer at the end, and you let it figure out the intermediate steps for itself. That's not a complicated idea. People were talking about it in 2020, 2021. So my expectation was that it would show up fairly quickly after the first big pretrained models.

And the reason it didn't, I think, comes down to a few things that are kind of boring individually but compound.

The first is that the base models weren't good enough yet. If your model essentially never gets the right answer on a hard problem, then the reward signal is almost all zeros and there's nothing to learn from. You need the model to be succeeding some reasonable fraction of the time before RL can amplify that. So there's a threshold effect. Below some level of base capability, the whole thing just doesn't take off, and it looks like the method doesn't work, when really you're just under the threshold.

The second is that it's quite easy to do this badly and conclude it's a dead end. The early attempts tended to collapse, or the model would learn to game whatever verifier you had, or you'd get a small bump and then plateau. And in a research org, a small bump that plateaus is a reason to move on to the next thing. So I think a lot of groups tried a version of it, saw something unimpressive, and put it down. The gap between "this basically works" and "this works well enough to justify a large fraction of your compute" turned out to be a lot of engineering, and engineering is slower than ideas.

And then the third thing, which I underweighted, is that the organisational incentives weren't pointed at it. For a few years the clearest path to a better model was just scaling pretraining. That was reliable, you could predict it with scaling laws, and it was what the leadership of these labs wanted to bet on. RL on reasoning was higher variance. It needed people willing to spend a lot of compute on something that might not pan out, and it needed good verifiable environments, which meant maths and code first and everything else later. That's a kind of social and infrastructural precondition that I wasn't really modelling when I was thinking about it purely as a technical question.

So I'd summarise it as: the idea was right, but I was treating it as an idea rather than as a system. Ideas can be true for years before the surrounding capability, engineering, and institutional will line up. And from a safety point of view that's actually a slightly uncomfortable lesson, because it means I should expect other things that currently look like they don't work to suddenly start working once the preconditions are met, and I may not get much warning.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger base models need to get hard problems right often enough to provide a useful reward signal, creating a threshold for RL. It does not communicate that improved models gain error-correction ability.

astra-6.text:
I think I underestimated how much had to work before that approach became useful. The basic idea is straightforward: let the model think for a while, check whether it got the right answer, and use reinforcement learning to make successful reasoning more likely. But if the model almost never gets the answer right in the first place, that signal doesn’t give you much to learn from. You need a sufficiently capable starting model, tasks where you can reliably check the answers, and a training setup that works well enough to put those pieces together.

Long reasoning traces also make credit assignment harder. If you reward an answer after a lot of intermediate steps, which of those steps should become more likely? And are you learning something useful, or just exploiting a weakness in how the answer is scored?

So my best explanation is that I was moving too quickly from “there’s a simple algorithmic idea here” to “this should work soon.” I’m less certain about which practical bottleneck accounted for most of the delay.

r001.rationale: The response says a sufficiently capable starting model is needed, but it does not connect improving pretrained models to reaching an error-correction threshold for long-trace reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I underestimated how much had to work at the same time. The basic idea is quite simple: let the model think for a while, check whether it got the right answer, and reinforce the reasoning that led to success. But that only gives you a useful learning signal if the model can already find successful answers often enough. If it almost never succeeds, you’re mostly getting a lot of failures without much information about what to do differently.

So you need a sufficiently capable starting model, problems at the right level of difficulty, and a way of checking the answers that the model can’t easily exploit. Then you have to make the reinforcement learning work reliably over these long sequences, which is expensive and introduces a lot of engineering complications.

My expectation was that the simplicity of the idea would translate into it happening sooner. In retrospect, that was too quick a jump. Having a plausible algorithmic story and having all the ingredients come together in a system that actually learns are quite different things.

r001.rationale: The response says a sufficiently capable starting model must find successful answers often enough to provide a useful learning signal. It does not mention pretrained models gaining error-correction ability or that ability reaching a threshold.
